strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: most prior shadow detectors output a single unified mask or ignore attached shadows entirely; this paper explicitly separates cast and attached shadows and grounds the separation in a physical model relating surface normals and light direction.

The iterative closed-loop design (shadow detection <-> light estimation) is well motivated and clearly explained, with a geometry-derived partial attached-shadow map used as an interpretable intermediate signal that is fed back into the detector.

Contributes a new curated dataset (1,458 images) built from three existing benchmarks (WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) with explicit, manually corrected cast/attached/undefined annotations, normal maps, and light directions — a useful resource for future work in this under-annotated area.

Strong empirical results: consistent improvement on full and attached-shadow BER/F1 versus 7 competitive baselines (including retrained variants), with at least 33% reduction in attached BER while maintaining competitive cast performance.

Comprehensive ablations isolate the contribution of surface-normal guidance, number of refinement iterations, and each individual loss term, and results are consistent with the paper's stated claims (geometry provides the largest single gain; iterations saturate around 3).

Practical downstream validation via shadow removal with a human preference study (80.7% prefer separate attached/cast refinement), plus cross-dataset qualitative generalization to SRD, SBU-TimeLapse, and ViSha, supporting real-world usefulness beyond the curated benchmark.

Limitations (dependence on off-the-shelf normal estimation, single-directional-light assumption) are explicitly and honestly discussed rather than omitted, and the supplementary material provides substantial additional detail on dataset construction, architecture, and inference overhead, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Ground-truth light directions for SOBA and CUHK are only heuristic estimates derived from object/shadow centroid displacement and coarse depth difference, not verified real light directions; this introduces label noise into both training supervision and quantitative light-direction evaluation (only WSRD has calibrated ground truth, and light-direction accuracy is validated on just 42 test images).

The method's cast-shadow BER (5.04) is not actually better than the best prior fine-tuned baseline (SILT: 4.52), and the paper's own text concedes cast BER is merely "comparable," so the claimed overall superiority rests mainly on attached and full-shadow metrics.

The geometric priors (surface normals) are derived from an off-the-shelf monocular depth model, and the paper acknowledges predictions degrade when these normals are inaccurate (Fig. 10); no quantitative sensitivity analysis of performance versus normal-estimation quality is provided.

Single dominant directional light assumption limits applicability to multi-light, indoor, or diffuse/soft-shadow scenes, which the authors note but do not empirically probe (e.g., no evaluation on an indoor or multi-light benchmark).

Architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the shadow-detection backbone reuses SILT with additional input channels, and the light estimator reuses ConvNeXt-S; the core contribution is the iterative feedback scheme and multi-task losses rather than a fundamentally new architecture.

Iterative inference adds meaningful computational cost (0.545s vs 0.176s non-iterative per image, and training requires 2 GPUs vs 1 for baselines), which is disclosed but not deeply analyzed in terms of accuracy/efficiency trade-offs beyond the ablation table.

Annotation quality for the new dataset relies on manual correction of heuristic/model-derived masks without reported inter-annotator agreement or annotation protocol validation, leaving some uncertainty about label reliability, especially for the excluded "undefined" shadow regions which could bias cast/attached metrics by removing ambiguous, harder pixels from evaluation.
